rationale: A wins because it keeps three real shapes and does not inflate the announcement into an industry obituary. A's "Rivian's next revenue line is selling electricity to everyone else's EVs" turns the update into a defensible P&L question with the proof list attached. B's "Every new Rivian stall will carry both plugs - the connector fight is over" is exactly the kind of sweeping standards claim a reporter will make you prove, and these facts do not prove it.
gaps_in_A: "why no automaker deal was struck" is a shade too strong; the update says no partnership was announced, not that a deal was sought, rejected, or strategically avoided.
"whether 'improves utilization' is a polite way of saying stalls sit empty" is a good sharp question, but it needs utilization data before anyone lets it harden into framing.

"whether opening the network dilutes a perk existing owners bought into" is useful only if Rivian previously sold the network as owner-exclusive; A flags that proof need, but the angle should not imply owner backlash without it.
gaps_in_B: "the connector fight is over" is unsupported category drama. One dual-plug commitment from Rivian does not settle the CCS/NACS transition.
"joining the small set of automaker-owned networks that sell to non-owners" imports outside market context not present in the update; it may be true, but this exercise did not give it to you.
"competing for the same drivers rather than negotiating with their manufacturers" turns "no partnership announced" into motive and strategy. That is how you get corrected after publication.

"four distinct shapes exist" overstates the set. The standards angle needs an outside peg and independent data before it is pitch-ready; from these facts alone, it is a sub-angle, not a full fourth lane.
